title: Etiquette
intro: US baseline is fine; tipping norms are nearly opposite (no tip in China, soft tip in Vietnam). Photo rules at temples, dress codes, and polite food refusal matter. China→Vietnam shift is noticeable but navigable.

tables.caption: China Survival Phrases (Mandarin)
rows: Néng bāng wǒ jiào Dīdī ma?
Can you call me a DiDi?

bullets.heading: China — Key Norms (Beijing)
items: Don't tip (exception: tour guides/porters ¥20–50/day; 5-star hotel staff follow international norms)
Two hands for business cards/gifts; inspect before putting away
Decline food firmly if needed: "我吃饱了" (I'm full); multiple declines expected
No photos where 禁止拍照 signs; ask at temples; dress modestly (shoulders/knees)
Bargain in markets (start 20–30% of ask); fixed price in malls/restaurants
Open hand to gesture; don't point; restaurant loudness is normal, not rude

bullets.heading: Vietnam — Key Norms
items: Tip softly: 10–15% table service; round up at stalls; $1–2/person/day for guides/drivers
Remove shoes at temples; dress modestly (sarongs often available)
Don't touch heads; eldest served/seated first at family tables
Cross streets at steady pace—motorbikes flow around you; don't freeze or rush
Don't raise voice publicly; resolve disputes quietly (face/thể diện matters)
Haggle at markets with a smile; V-sign in photos is friendly, not political

bullets.heading: Gestures & Taboos
items: China avoid: clock gifts, green hats, chopsticks upright in rice, Taiwan/Tibet politics
Vietnam avoid: index-finger pointing, crossed fingers in photos, feet toward people, finger-snapping servers
Both: thumbs up and OK sign acceptable in both countries

bullets.heading: Supporting Locals
items: China: hutong artisan shops over tourist stalls; local restaurants vs Tiananmen tourist spots; DiDi over exploitative ride-hail
Vietnam: boutique Hội An hotels; buy from Kim Bong/Thanh Ha artisans; local coffee shops vs Highlands chain; tip Grab drivers

callouts.text: Tipping flip: no tip in China (except guides/porters); 10–15% appreciated in Vietnam
Cultural whiplash buffer: Vietnam feels warmer and more English-friendly—slow down, smile, linger (tà tà)
Mindset shift at border: Beijing = efficiency; Vietnam = relationships
